source.title: Investigating Neural Scaling Laws Emerging from Deep Data Structure

record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own scaling experiments, including settings where expected scaling appears only over narrow ranges or fails to appear, and argues that the behavior depends on data structure and target-function properties.
record.gate_note: The study tests scaling in synthetic data and student-teacher settings, not language-model pretraining. Predictions and findings cited from other papers are not recorded as results. Intrinsic-dimension estimates and teacher-function visualizations are not rows because they do not measure a scaling outcome. The text also notes optimization and hyperparameter-tuning difficulties, but reports no separate numerical outcome for those difficulties.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own data-scaling experiments with neural student-teacher regression on synthetic manifold and fractal data. That is a new setting, and it reports whether power-law scaling appears and over what range. This bears on V5, not on language-model pretraining.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that the intrinsic dimension and geometry of the data, and the genericness of the target function, may both shape neural scaling laws. They add that reproducing neural scaling results was difficult, hinting at a volatile process that depends on these factors. They frame this as more questions than answers.
record.recipe_differences: Uses synthetic percolation-cluster data, nonparametric regression, and neural student-teacher experiments rather than language-model pretraining loss sweeps over parameters, tokens, and compute.
record.method_sensitivity: Scaling outcomes are reported to relate to teacher-function construction and nonlinearity; increasing random ReLU teacher depth appeared to help, while increasing width did not change scaling. Fourier teachers with max_freq=1 showed the expected behavior only over a limited range.

fits_no_version.finding: 1-NN regression on an embedded percolation cluster gives slope -0.49 against the predicted -0.5. The result does not change with embedding dimension or branching factor.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Nonparametric regression error scales with data as predicted by the data's intrinsic (fractal) dimension.

fits_no_version.finding: Scaling behaviour tracked teacher non-linearity. Wider ReLU teachers did not change scaling.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Whether neural data scaling matches manifold-dimension theory depends on the genericness or non-linearity of the target function.

record.problems: The experiments use synthetic settings, several reported neural-network ranges are narrow, initial attempts did not yield expected slopes, and key values for sweeps are not given in the text. The authors also report noisy intrinsic-dimension measurements and difficulty with optimization and hyperparameter tuning.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible scaling results were left out. Intrinsic-dimension estimator results and visual descriptions of teacher functions were omitted because they do not report a scaling outcome.

untested.parts: All of it: no language-model pretraining loss.
All of it: student architecture is not varied at fixed parameter count.
All of it: no comparison of language-model fits or fitting choices.
Image and video models, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer, and parameter or compute scaling. Only data scaling in synthetic regression is tested.

record.verdict_notes: This is an informal LessWrong project write-up. Hyperparameter and optimisation difficulties confound the neural results, and the authors are skeptical of the narrow-range results. The expected slopes come from Sharma & Kaplan manifold theory rather than the original sources, so the slope mismatches bear on that theory more than on V5's power-law form. Tranche changed from T5 to T3: the study argues no version is wrong, it reports a new setting.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss scaling in parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether fits from small runs predict runs orders of magnitude larger.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocations and their growth with compute.
Loss differences across architectures at a fixed parameter count.
Image and video models, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, and transfer.
Downstream task performance and its relationship to scale or pretraining loss.
Systematic variation of parameter-counting conventions, training schedules, fitting methods, and compute-optimal allocation; comparison of published language-model exponents.
